newsitem.title: SIERRA LEONE: Sierra Leone militia battles hunger, disease.
newsitem.headline: Sierra Leone militia battles hunger, disease.

text.p: Traditional foes hunger and disease are a greater enemy than rebels or the army in southeast Sierra Leone, where a civilian militia loyal to the ousted president announced a ceasefire on Saturday.

Kamajor commanders said despite the turmoil in the capital Freetown, where rebels of the Revolutionary United Front (RUF) have joined forces with troops who toppled President Ahmad Tejan Kabbah last weekend, their priority was finding food and burying the dead.
"Fighting has ceased but everyone is fighting another war against hunger and disease," said Victor Pabai, a former aid worker and local resident.
"We are dropping the guns this week through next week to find some food for the people and bury the dead," said Kamajor commander Eddie Massally.

He said they had opened the border with Liberia and the road through to the Siera Leonean town of Kenema in the hope of allowing people to trade. A few rusty pickups carrying petty traders passed through militia roadblocks on Saturday heading into Liberia.
A group of junior officers led by Major Johnny Paul Koromah seized power last Sunday, saying they wanted to bring the RUF into government to end the civil war which began in 1991.
One of their first acts was to ban the Kamajors, on whom Kabbah had come to depend in battles against the rebels.

There have been clashes between Kamajors and the army, and many soldiers resent the resources they have received from the presidency. The deputy defence minister in the ousted government, Hinga Norman, is a former Kamajor.

The area around Jedema, close to the Liberian border, was cut off by battles between Kamajors and the RUF last September. The fighting forced thousands of people across the border into Liberia, where conditions were scarcely better.
The rebels and Kabbah's government signed a peace accord last November, and the United Nations began repatriating refugees to Sierra Leone from Liberia last February.
They were resettled at a camp near Freetown and later made their way to their original villages inland.

But the villagers have begun trickling back to Liberia again to escape starvation and disease. There are no functioning health clinics nearby, and villagers subsist on a diet of cassava and bush yams.
"Since Monday we have buried 13 dead bodies, all died from starvation or cholera," Pabai said.

The Kamajors seemed to have abandoned plans declared earlier this week to march on Freetown to reinstate Kabbah, but with West African states flying troops into Freetown, there were growing signs that Nigeria and its allies would do it for them.
